newsitem.title: USA: Cabletron sell-off costs founders $600 million.
newsitem.headline: Cabletron sell-off costs founders $600 million.

text.p: Cabletron Systems Inc. shares lost a third of their value Tuesday after the computer network equipment maker warned of disappointing earnings and wiped out $605 million of the net worth of its two founders.

Cabletron, which makes equipment known as hubs and switches used to connect computer networks, was hammered on Wall Street as its shares fell $15.625 to $30.125 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most active stock.
The sell-off followed the company's warning late Monday that its results for the quarter ended in May were likely to fall substantially short of Wall Street expectations.
But even after that hefty loss, the founders, Chairman Craig Benson and Chief Executive Robert Levine, hold a joint stake in the company valued at $1.18 billion.
"That's something I don't track because it goes up and down every day," Benson said when asked to comment on the steep decline in the potential value of his stock holdings.

"I am personally more worried about making sure that the company's on track," he said, after spending much of Tuesday in meetings with Cabletron managers and in consultation with Wall Street analysts. "That's been the focus of my day today."

Cabletron said Monday it expected results for the first quarter ended in May to "meet or slightly exceed" the $57 million, or 37 cents a share, in the May 1996 quarter, which was restated for acquisitions and a stock split.
That figure was well shy of the latest financial analysts' consensus estimate of $78.5 million, or 50 cents per share.
For Benson and Levine the news was especially bad.
They earn salaries of $52,000 a year and don't receive any stock options, unlike the hefty bonuses of many other executives.

Benson, 42, and Levine, 39, founded Cabletron in 1983 in Rochester, N.H. They still see themselves as local "owner operators," in contrast to the typical hired managers brought in to run most large companies.

The two -- who have funded the company out of the profits it has generated in the course of growing to become a $1.4 billion concern in the most recent fiscal year -- pride themselves on never having accepted venture capital funding.
Cabletron's troubles were not isolated Tuesday.
The warning also sent a shiver through technology stocks, which fuelled fears that Cabletron's problems may be part of a wider slowdown in computer industry growth.

Leading chip maker Intel Corp. was down $4.75 at $145 a share on Nasdaq. Seagate Technology Inc. fell $3.75 to $38.625 and Compaq Computer Corp., the leading maker of personal computers, slid $7.375 to $100, both on the NYSE.

Cabletron blamed product transition issues and a sales shortfall in its European operations for its lackluster results but said it needed more data to give a fuller picture of the causes of the shortfall.
David Kirkpatrick, Cabletron's chief financial officer, said in a phone interview Tuesday that the results were principally due to sluggish international sales results.
